lessons.title: Energy Stores & Transfers
lessons.description: Eight energy stores, how energy transfers between stores through mechanical, thermal, radiation and electrical pathways, and energy transfer diagrams.
lessons.content_html:
Energy Stores

Everything in the universe involves energy. Energy is not a substance you can hold; it is a quantity that describes the capacity of a system to do work. In GCSE physics, we describe energy using the idea of energy stores. There are eight energy stores you need to know:

Kinetic — energy of a moving object. Gravitational potential — energy stored when an object is raised above the ground. Elastic potential — energy stored when an object is stretched or compressed. Thermal — energy related to the temperature of an object. Chemical — energy stored in bonds between atoms (fuels, food, batteries). Magnetic — energy of magnets attracting or repelling. Electrostatic — energy of charged particles attracting or repelling. Nuclear — energy stored in the nucleus of an atom.

Key Fact

The eight energy stores are: kinetic, gravitational potential, elastic potential, thermal, chemical, magnetic, electrostatic, and nuclear.

Energy Transfers

Energy can be transferred between stores by four main pathways:

Mechanically — a force acting on an object does work and transfers energy (e.g. pushing a trolley transfers energy from chemical stores in your muscles to kinetic stores in the trolley). Electrically — charges flowing through a circuit transfer energy (e.g. from the chemical store of a battery to the thermal store of a filament lamp). By heating — energy transfers from a hotter object to a cooler one by conduction, convection, or evaporation. By radiation — energy is transferred by electromagnetic waves, such as light or infrared radiation from the Sun.

Key Fact

The four energy transfer pathways are: mechanically (by forces doing work), electrically (by charges in a circuit), by heating (conduction, convection, evaporation), and by radiation (electromagnetic waves).

Energy Transfers in Systems

A system is an object or group of objects. When a system changes, energy is transferred between stores. Here are some important examples from the specification:

When a ball is thrown upwards, energy is transferred from the kinetic store to the gravitational potential energy store. As the ball rises, it slows down: kinetic energy decreases while gravitational potential energy increases. At the highest point, all the kinetic energy has been transferred to gravitational potential energy (ignoring air resistance). On the way down, the reverse happens.

When a car crashes into a barrier, energy is transferred from the kinetic store to the thermal store (the car and barrier heat up) and to the elastic potential store (the car body deforms). Some energy is also transferred by sound waves to the thermal store of the surroundings.

When a constant force accelerates a car along a road, energy is transferred from the chemical store of the fuel to the kinetic store of the car. Some energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings through friction and air resistance.

Drawing Energy Transfer Diagrams

Energy transfer diagrams use boxes to represent energy stores and arrows to show the transfer pathway. The width of each arrow can show the relative amount of energy transferred along that pathway. For example, boiling water in a kettle: the chemical store of the electricity supply transfers energy electrically to the thermal store of the water (useful) and to the thermal store of the surroundings (wasted, through heating of the kettle body and sound).

When drawing these diagrams, always label each store clearly and show the transfer pathway on or beside the arrow. The total energy in must equal the total energy out — this links directly to the principle of conservation of energy.

Key Fact

Energy transfer diagrams show energy stores as labelled boxes and transfer pathways as arrows. The total energy in always equals the total energy out.

Exam Tip: When describing energy changes, always name the store energy is transferred from, the store it goes to, and the pathway (mechanically, electrically, by heating, or by radiation). Vague answers like “energy is lost” lose marks — say “energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings by heating.”

Energy is stored in eight different stores and transferred between them by four pathways. Being able to describe these changes precisely — naming stores and pathways — is essential for almost every energy question on the exam.

practice_questions.text: Compare the energy transfers that occur when a car accelerates along a flat road with those when a car drives up a steep hill at constant speed.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Both: energy is transferred from the chemical store of the fuel (1)
• Flat road: energy goes to the kinetic store of the car (1)
• Hill: energy goes to the gravitational potential energy store (as the car gains height) (1)

practice_questions.text: A student says ‘energy is lost when a light bulb is switched on.’ Explain why this statement is not correct.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Energy cannot be created or destroyed / conservation of energy (1)
• Energy is transferred from the chemical/electrical store to the thermal store of the surroundings (1)
• The energy is dissipated (spread out) rather than lost — it is no longer in a useful form (1).

practice_questions.text: A battery-powered toy car is switched on and travels across a table before falling off the edge. Describe the energy transfers and changes in energy stores from the moment the car is switched on until it hits the ground.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• Chemical store of the battery transfers energy electrically to the kinetic store of the car
• Some energy dissipated to thermal store of surroundings by heating (friction)
• As car leaves the table edge, energy is transferred from the gravitational potential store
• Gravitational potential energy decreases as height decreases
• Kinetic energy increases as the car speeds up while falling
• On impact, kinetic energy is transferred to thermal and elastic potential stores (deformation/sound)

lessons.title: Conservation of Energy & Energy Resources
lessons.description: Conservation of energy, gravitational potential energy, kinetic energy, efficiency, and energy resources.
lessons.content_html:
Conservation of Energy

The conservation of energy is one of the most important ideas in physics. It states that energy cannot be created or destroyed — only transferred from one store to another. The total energy in a closed system always stays the same.

Key Fact

Energy cannot be created or destroyed. In a closed system, the total energy before a change is always equal to the total energy after the change.

Calculating Gravitational Potential Energy

When an object is raised above the ground, energy is transferred to its gravitational potential energy store. The amount of energy stored depends on the mass, the gravitational field strength, and the height gained:

\(\Delta GPE = m \times g \times \Delta h\)

Where \(\Delta GPE\) is the change in gravitational potential energy in joules (J), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), \(g\) is gravitational field strength in newtons per kilogram (N/kg), and \(\Delta h\) is the change in vertical height in metres (m). On Earth, \(g \approx 9.8\) N/kg.

A 2 kg book is lifted 1.5 m onto a shelf. Calculate the change in gravitational potential energy. Use \(g = 9.8\) N/kg.

\(\Delta GPE = m \times g \times \Delta h = 2 \times 9.8 \times 1.5 = 29.4\) J

Calculating Kinetic Energy

The energy in the kinetic energy store of a moving object depends on its mass and the square of its speed:

\(KE = \frac{1}{2} \times m \times v^2\)

Where \(KE\) is kinetic energy in joules (J), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), and \(v\) is speed in metres per second (m/s). Because speed is squared, doubling the speed quadruples the kinetic energy.

A 0.5 kg ball travels at 4 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.

\(KE = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.5 \times 4^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.5 \times 16 = 4\) J

Wasted Energy and Efficiency

No energy transfer is perfectly efficient. Some energy is always dissipated — spread out to the thermal store of the surroundings. This wasted energy cannot easily be recovered. Mechanical processes become wasteful when friction causes a rise in temperature, heating the surroundings.

We can reduce unwanted energy transfers by lubrication (reducing friction between moving parts) and thermal insulation (reducing energy transfer by heating). For example, loft insulation and cavity wall insulation reduce the rate at which a building cools by trapping air, which is a poor thermal conductor.

Key Fact

Efficiency measures how much of the input energy is usefully transferred: \(\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful energy output}}{\text{total energy input}}\). Efficiency has no units and is always between 0 and 1 (or 0% and 100%).

Energy Resources

The main energy resources available on Earth are: non-renewable sources (fossil fuels — coal, oil, natural gas — and nuclear fuel) and renewable sources (wind, solar, hydroelectric, tidal, geothermal, wave, and bio-fuel).

Non-renewable resources release large amounts of energy per kilogram and provide a reliable supply. However, burning fossil fuels produces carbon dioxide (contributing to climate change) and they will eventually run out. Nuclear fuel produces radioactive waste that must be stored safely.

Renewable resources will not run out and most produce no greenhouse gases during operation. However, many are intermittent (wind and solar depend on weather conditions), and some require large land areas or have visual/noise impacts. Bio-fuels are carbon neutral in theory because the plants absorb CO\(_2\) as they grow.

The global trend is a shift towards renewable energy sources. This is driven by concerns about climate change, energy security (reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels), and the falling cost of renewable technologies such as solar panels and wind turbines.

Key Fact

Non-renewable resources (fossil fuels and nuclear) provide reliable, high-energy output but produce waste and will run out. Renewable resources (wind, solar, tidal, hydroelectric, geothermal, bio-fuel, wave) are replenished naturally but many are intermittent.

Exam Tip: Calculation questions on energy are very common. Always write the equation, substitute the values with correct units, then calculate. Show every step — you can pick up method marks even if you make an arithmetic error. Remember that \(v\) in the kinetic energy equation is squared, so always square the speed before multiplying.

The conservation of energy principle underpins all energy calculations. You need to recall and use the equations for gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy, understand efficiency, and be able to compare renewable and non-renewable energy resources.

• Therefore no real device can be 100% efficient

lessons.title: Current, Potential Difference & Resistance
lessons.description: Electric charge, current, potential difference, resistance, I–V characteristics, and the behaviour of thermistors and light-dependent resistors.
lessons.content_html:
Electric Charge and Current

Electric current is the rate of flow of charge around a circuit. In metals, the current is carried by electrons, which are negatively charged. When a potential difference is applied across a circuit, electrons flow from the negative terminal of the battery through the wires and components to the positive terminal.

Current is measured in amperes (A) using an ammeter, which is always connected in series with the component being measured.

Key Fact

Charge, current, and time are linked by the equation: \(Q = I \times t\), where \(Q\) is charge in coulombs (C), \(I\) is current in amperes (A), and \(t\) is time in seconds (s).

Potential Difference

Potential difference (often called voltage) is the energy transferred per unit charge that passes between two points in a circuit. One volt means one joule of energy is transferred for every coulomb of charge that passes. It is measured using a voltmeter, which is always connected in parallel across the component being measured.

The equation linking energy transferred, charge, and potential difference is:

\(E = Q \times V\)

Where \(E\) is energy transferred in joules (J), \(Q\) is charge in coulombs (C), and \(V\) is potential difference in volts (V).

Resistance

Resistance is a measure of how difficult it is for charge to flow through a component. A high resistance means less current flows for a given potential difference. Resistance is measured in ohms (\(\Omega\)).

The relationship between potential difference, current, and resistance is given by:

\(V = I \times R\)

Where \(V\) is potential difference in volts (V), \(I\) is current in amperes (A), and \(R\) is resistance in ohms (\(\Omega\)). This can be rearranged to \(I = \frac{V}{R}\) or \(R = \frac{V}{I}\).

A resistor has a resistance of 20 \(\Omega\). The current through it is 0.5 A. Calculate the potential difference across it.

\(V = I \times R = 0.5 \times 20 = 10\) V

Key Fact

The three core circuit equations are: \(V = I \times R\) (Ohm’s law), \(Q = I \times t\) (charge), and \(E = Q \times V\) (energy transferred).

I–V Characteristics

The relationship between current and potential difference can be shown on an I–V graph. Different components produce different characteristic graphs:

Fixed resistor: The I–V graph is a straight line through the origin. Current is directly proportional to potential difference, meaning the resistance stays constant. This component obeys Ohm’s law.

Filament lamp: The graph is a curve that becomes less steep at higher potential differences. As the current increases, the filament heats up, which increases its resistance. The lamp does not obey Ohm’s law.

Diode: Current flows in one direction only (forward bias). In reverse bias, essentially no current flows. The I–V graph shows current increasing rapidly once the threshold voltage (about 0.7 V for silicon) is reached in the forward direction, and zero current in the reverse direction.

Thermistors and LDRs

Some components have a resistance that changes with conditions:

Thermistor (NTC type) — resistance decreases as temperature increases. Used in temperature sensors and thermostats. LDR (light-dependent resistor) — resistance decreases as light intensity increases. Used in automatic lighting systems and light meters.

Key Fact

Thermistor (NTC): resistance decreases as temperature increases. LDR: resistance decreases as light intensity increases. Both are used as sensors in control circuits.

Exam Tip: Always connect an ammeter in series and a voltmeter in parallel. If asked to draw a circuit to investigate resistance, include a battery, ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel across the component, and a variable resistor to change the current.

Current, potential difference, and resistance are the three fundamental quantities in circuit physics. Master the equations \(V = I \times R\), \(Q = I \times t\), and \(E = Q \times V\), and understand how different components (fixed resistors, filament lamps, diodes, thermistors, and LDRs) behave.

practice_questions.text: A student uses a circuit with a battery, ammeter, voltmeter, variable resistor, and a fixed resistor to investigate the I–V characteristics of the fixed resistor. Describe the method the student should use and explain what the results would show.

• For a fixed resistor (at constant temperature) the graph is a straight line through the origin

• The gradient of the line gives 1/R (the reciprocal of resistance)

lessons.title: Series & Parallel Circuits
lessons.description: Series and parallel circuits, current and potential difference distribution, resistance calculation, and electrical power in circuits.
lessons.content_html:
Series Circuits

In a series circuit, all components are connected end to end in a single loop. There is only one path for the current to follow.

In a series circuit:

Current is the same through every component. There is only one path, so the same charge flows through each part: \(I_{\text{total}} = I_1 = I_2 = I_3\).

Potential difference is shared between the components. The total potential difference of the supply equals the sum of the potential differences across each component: \(V_{\text{total}} = V_1 + V_2 + V_3\).

Resistance adds up. The total resistance is the sum of the individual resistances: \(R_{\text{total}} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3\).

Key Fact

In a series circuit: current is the same everywhere, potential differences add up to the supply voltage, and resistances add up.

Two resistors of 10 \(\Omega\) and 20 \(\Omega\) are connected in series to a 6 V battery. Calculate the total resistance and the current in the circuit.

Total resistance: \(R_{\text{total}} = 10 + 20 = 30 \; \Omega\)

Current: \(I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{6}{30} = 0.2\) A

Parallel Circuits

In a parallel circuit, components are connected across each other on separate branches. The current has more than one path to follow.

In a parallel circuit:

Current splits at junctions. The total current from the supply equals the sum of the currents through each branch: \(I_{\text{total}} = I_1 + I_2 + I_3\). Current is conserved at every junction.

Potential difference is the same across each branch. Every component connected in parallel has the same potential difference across it: \(V_{\text{total}} = V_1 = V_2 = V_3\).

Resistance decreases. Adding more branches gives the current more paths to flow through, so the total resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistance.

Key Fact

In a parallel circuit: the potential difference is the same across each branch, currents through each branch add up to the total current, and the total resistance is less than the smallest individual resistance.

Two resistors are connected in parallel to a 12 V battery. One has a resistance of 6 \(\Omega\) and the other 12 \(\Omega\). Calculate the current through each resistor and the total current.

Both resistors have 12 V across them (parallel circuit rule).

Current through 6 \(\Omega\) resistor: \(I_1 = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{12}{6} = 2\) A

Current through 12 \(\Omega\) resistor: \(I_2 = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{12}{12} = 1\) A

Total current: \(I_{\text{total}} = 2 + 1 = 3\) A

Energy in Circuits

When charge flows through a resistor, the electrical energy is transferred to the thermal store of the resistor, which heats up. This happens because the moving electrons collide with the metal ions in the lattice, transferring energy to them and making them vibrate more. This energy is then dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings.

We can reduce unwanted heating by using wires with lower resistance. Thicker wires and shorter wires have lower resistance, which means less energy is wasted as heat.

Electrical Power

Power is the rate at which energy is transferred, measured in watts (W). One watt equals one joule of energy transferred per second. There are three key power equations:

\(P = \frac{E}{t}\) — power equals energy transferred divided by time

\(P = I \times V\) — power equals current times potential difference

\(P = I^2 \times R\) — power equals current squared times resistance

A heater has a current of 3 A and a resistance of 40 \(\Omega\). Calculate the power of the heater.

\(P = I^2 \times R = 3^2 \times 40 = 9 \times 40 = 360\) W

Key Fact

The three power equations are: \(P = \frac{E}{t}\), \(P = I \times V\), and \(P = I^2 \times R\). Choose the equation that uses the values you are given in the question.

Exam Tip: Learn the series and parallel rules as a set of contrasts. In series, current stays the same and voltages add up. In parallel, voltage stays the same and currents add up. Examiners frequently test whether you can apply these rules to unfamiliar circuits.

Series and parallel circuits follow clear, predictable rules. Knowing how current, potential difference, and resistance behave in each type of circuit — and being able to calculate power and energy transfer — is essential for the electricity section of the exam.

lessons.title: Domestic Uses of Electricity & Power
lessons.description: Electrical energy transfer, power calculations, mains wiring, fuses, and safety hazards of domestic electricity supply.
lessons.content_html:
Energy Transferred by Electrical Devices

Every electrical device transfers energy from one store to another. A kettle transfers energy from the electrical store to the thermal store of water. A motor transfers energy from the electrical store to the kinetic store. Understanding how much energy a device transfers — and how quickly — is essential for calculating running costs and choosing appropriate safety features.

The energy transferred by a device depends on three things: the current flowing through it, the potential difference across it, and how long it runs for. These are linked by the equation:

$$E = I \times V \times t$$

where \(E\) is energy transferred in joules (J), \(I\) is current in amperes (A), \(V\) is potential difference in volts (V), and \(t\) is time in seconds (s). For example, a heater drawing 10 A at 230 V for 60 seconds transfers \(10 \times 230 \times 60 = 138{,}000\) J of energy.

Key Fact

Energy transferred (J) = current (A) × potential difference (V) × time (s). You must be able to recall and rearrange this equation.

Electrical Power

Power tells you how fast a device transfers energy. It is measured in watts (W), where one watt equals one joule of energy transferred per second. A 2000 W kettle transfers 2000 J every second — much faster than a 60 W lamp, which transfers only 60 J per second.

Power is calculated using:

$$P = \frac{E}{t}$$

where \(P\) is power in watts (W), \(E\) is energy transferred in joules (J), and \(t\) is time in seconds (s).

Two more equations link power to current, potential difference, and resistance:

$$P = I \times V$$

$$P = I^2 \times R$$

The second equation shows that doubling the current quadruples the power dissipated, because current is squared. This is why high-current devices need thicker cables — thin wires carrying large currents would overheat dangerously.

Key Fact

Three power equations to recall: \(P = \frac{E}{t}\), \(P = I \times V\), and \(P = I^2 \times R\). Each connects power to different electrical quantities.

Direct Current and Alternating Current

There are two types of electric current. Direct current (d.c.) is the movement of charge in one direction only. Cells and batteries supply d.c. — the current always flows from the positive terminal, through the circuit, and back to the negative terminal.

Alternating current (a.c.) is different: the direction of charge flow keeps reversing. In the UK, the mains electricity supply is a.c. at a frequency of 50 Hz (meaning the current changes direction 50 times per second) and a voltage of about 230 V.

Alternating current can be easily stepped up to very high voltages for efficient long-distance transmission through the National Grid, then stepped back down for safe domestic use. Transformers, which only work with a.c., make this possible. Direct current cannot be transformed in the same way, which is why a.c. became the standard for mains supply.

The Three-Pin Plug and Mains Wiring

Domestic appliances connect to the mains through a three-pin plug containing three colour-coded wires:

The live wire (brown) carries the alternating current to the appliance. Its potential alternates between about +230 V and −230 V relative to the neutral wire. This makes it dangerous even when a device is switched off — the live wire is still connected to the supply.

The neutral wire (blue) completes the circuit and carries current away from the appliance. It is at, or very close to, 0 V (earth potential).

The earth wire (green and yellow stripes) is a safety wire connected to the metal casing of an appliance. Under normal conditions, no current flows through it. If a fault occurs and the live wire touches the metal casing, the earth wire provides a low-resistance path for current to flow safely to earth, preventing electrocution.

Key Fact

Live wire = brown (alternates at ~230 V). Neutral wire = blue (~0 V). Earth wire = green and yellow (safety, connected to metal casing). The potential difference between live and neutral is about 230 V. Between live and earth it is also about 230 V. Between neutral and earth it is approximately 0 V.

Fuses and Circuit Breakers

A fuse is a thin wire inside a ceramic or glass case, placed in series with the live wire. If the current exceeds the fuse's rated value, the wire melts and breaks the circuit, cutting off the current before it can cause a fire or damage the appliance. Common fuse ratings are 3 A (for appliances up to about 700 W) and 13 A (for higher-power devices).

Fuses and switches must always be connected in the live wire, not the neutral wire. This ensures that when the fuse blows or the switch is off, no high voltage reaches the appliance — making it safe to touch or repair.

A circuit breaker does the same job but works faster and can be reset by flipping a switch, rather than needing to be replaced like a fuse.

If the fuse were in the neutral wire and it blew, the live wire would still be connected to the appliance. The metal casing could remain at 230 V, creating a serious electrocution risk. By placing the fuse in the live wire, blowing the fuse disconnects the high-voltage supply completely.

Power Ratings and Energy Use

Every domestic appliance has a power rating printed on it. A 2000 W kettle uses energy much faster than a 10 W LED bulb. Higher power means greater energy transfer per second, which usually means higher running costs.

Different appliances transfer energy in different ways. A toaster transfers electrical energy to thermal energy to heat bread. A washing machine transfers electrical energy to kinetic energy (the drum spinning) and thermal energy (heating the water). A television transfers electrical energy to light and sound energy.

To calculate the current drawn by an appliance, rearrange \(P = I \times V\) to give \(I = \frac{P}{V}\). For a 2000 W kettle on the 230 V mains: \(I = \frac{2000}{230} \approx 8.7\) A. This tells you a 13 A fuse is needed (the next standard rating above 8.7 A).

Calculate the normal operating current using \(I = \frac{P}{V}\), then choose the fuse with the next rating above this value. For a 700 W microwave: \(I = \frac{700}{230} \approx 3.0\) A, so a 3 A fuse is suitable. For a 2500 W heater: \(I = \frac{2500}{230} \approx 10.9\) A, so a 13 A fuse is needed. The fuse must be rated just above the normal current — too low and it blows during normal use; too high and it fails to protect.

Dangers of the Mains Supply

The mains supply at 230 V is potentially lethal. Any connection between the live wire and earth creates a direct path for current to flow through whatever — or whoever — completes that circuit. Touching the live wire while standing on the ground can cause a large current to pass through the body, which can cause burns, cardiac arrest, or death.

Even when a switch is off, the live wire inside the appliance may still be at 230 V. This is why you should always switch off and unplug an appliance before attempting any repairs, and why damaged cables or cracked plugs must be replaced immediately.

Key Fact

The live wire is dangerous because it carries a potential of ~230 V even when a switch is off. Any connection between live and earth can cause electrocution. Safety features include: fuses in the live wire, earth wires on metal-cased appliances, circuit breakers, and double insulation on plastic-cased devices.

Exam Tip

When asked to explain why a fuse must be in the live wire, always state that it disconnects the high-voltage supply from the appliance. Simply saying "it breaks the circuit" is not enough — you must explain that the appliance is no longer connected to 230 V.

Summary

Electrical power is the rate of energy transfer, measured in watts. The UK mains supply is a.c. at 230 V and 50 Hz. Domestic plugs have three wires (live, neutral, earth) with fuses and circuit breakers providing safety. Understanding power ratings helps you calculate current draw, choose the correct fuse, and compare energy use between appliances.

lessons.title: Static Electricity & Electric Fields
lessons.description: Atomic structure, electric charge, electron transfer, and how objects become charged through friction and contact.
lessons.content_html:
The Structure of the Atom and Electric Charge

All matter is made up of atoms. Each atom has a tiny, dense nucleus at its centre, made up of positively charged protons and uncharged neutrons. Orbiting the nucleus at set distances are negatively charged electrons.

The nuclear radius is much smaller than the radius of the atom as a whole — roughly 10,000 times smaller. Almost all of the atom’s mass is concentrated in the nucleus. In a neutral atom, the number of protons equals the number of electrons, so the overall charge is zero.

Key Fact

Proton: relative charge +1, relative mass 1. Neutron: relative charge 0, relative mass 1. Electron: relative charge −1, relative mass negligible (about 1/1836). In a neutral atom, the number of protons equals the number of electrons.

How Objects Become Charged

Objects become electrically charged when electrons are transferred between them. It is always electrons that move — protons are locked inside the nucleus and cannot transfer between objects. When two insulating materials are rubbed together, friction causes electrons to move from one surface to the other.

The material that gains electrons becomes negatively charged (it now has more electrons than protons). The material that loses electrons becomes positively charged (it now has more protons than electrons). The total charge is conserved — no charge is created or destroyed, only transferred.

For example, rubbing a polythene rod with a cloth causes electrons to transfer from the cloth to the rod. The rod gains electrons and becomes negatively charged. The cloth loses electrons and becomes positively charged. Rubbing an acetate rod with a cloth has the opposite effect — electrons move from the rod to the cloth, leaving the rod positively charged.

Protons are bound tightly inside the nucleus by the strong nuclear force and cannot be removed by rubbing. Electrons, however, orbit the nucleus in shells and the outermost electrons are held relatively weakly. Friction provides enough energy to dislodge these outer electrons and transfer them to another material.

Attraction and Repulsion

Charged objects exert forces on each other without touching — this is a non-contact force. The rule is straightforward:

Like charges repel — two positive objects push each other apart, as do two negative objects. Unlike charges attract — a positive and a negative object pull towards each other.

A charged object can also attract an uncharged object. This happens because the charge on the first object causes the electrons in the neutral object to redistribute: the opposite charge moves closer and the like charge moves further away, creating a net attractive force. This is called electrostatic induction.

Key Fact

Like charges repel, unlike charges attract. A charged object can also attract a neutral object through induction. These electrostatic forces are non-contact forces.

Electric Fields

An electric field is the region around a charged object where another charged object would experience a force. Every charged object creates an electric field in the space surrounding it. The field is strongest close to the charge and gets weaker with distance.

Electric field lines are used to represent the field. They always point from positive to negative. For a single positive charge, the field lines point outwards (away from the charge). For a single negative charge, the field lines point inwards (towards the charge). Between two oppositely charged parallel plates, the field lines are straight, evenly spaced, and point from the positive plate to the negative plate — this is a uniform electric field.

The closer together the field lines, the stronger the field at that point. Near a point charge, lines are bunched closely together; far away, they spread out, indicating a weaker field.

Objects can interact at a distance without contact through three types of field: gravitational fields (between masses), magnetic fields (between magnets or current-carrying conductors), and electrostatic fields (between charges). All three are non-contact forces. In each case, the force is transmitted through the field that surrounds the object.

Ions and Electron Transfer

When atoms lose or gain electrons, they become ions. An atom that loses one or more electrons becomes a positive ion (it has more protons than electrons). An atom that gains one or more electrons becomes a negative ion (it has more electrons than protons).

This process of electron transfer is fundamental to understanding both static electricity and the formation of ionic compounds. In metals, the outer electrons are free to move — this is what allows metals to conduct electricity. In insulators, electrons are fixed in position, so charge tends to build up on the surface rather than flowing away.

Static charge causes many familiar effects. Walking across a carpet in socks can cause electrons to transfer to your body, and touching a metal door handle creates a small spark as charge flows to earth. Lightning occurs when charge builds up in clouds through friction between ice particles and water droplets. Electrostatic charge is also used in practical applications such as spray painting (charged paint droplets are attracted to a grounded metal surface, giving an even coat) and photocopiers.

Key Fact

In conductors (metals), outer electrons are free to move, allowing charge to flow. In insulators, electrons are fixed in position, so charge builds up on the surface. Static charge is caused by the transfer of electrons between materials by friction.

Exam Tip

When explaining how an object becomes charged, always say that electrons are transferred — never say “charge is transferred” without specifying which type. Also be clear about the direction: state which material gains electrons (becomes negative) and which loses them (becomes positive).

Summary

Atoms contain protons (+1), neutrons (0), and electrons (−1). Objects become charged by the transfer of electrons, not protons. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. Electric fields surround charged objects — field lines point from positive to negative, and closer lines mean a stronger field. Conductors allow charge to flow; insulators allow charge to build up on their surface.

lessons.title: Particle Model & Density
lessons.description: The particle model of matter, states of matter, density, and practical methods for measuring density.
lessons.content_html:
The Particle Model of Matter

All matter is made up of tiny particles (atoms or molecules) that are constantly moving. The particle model (also called kinetic theory) explains the behaviour of solids, liquids, and gases by considering how these particles are arranged and how they move.

In a solid, particles are held in a fixed, regular arrangement by strong forces of attraction between them. The particles vibrate about fixed positions but cannot move from place to place. This is why solids have a definite shape and a definite volume.

In a liquid, the particles are still close together but are no longer in a fixed pattern. They can slide over and past one another, which is why liquids can flow and take the shape of their container. Liquids have a definite volume but no fixed shape.

In a gas, particles are far apart with almost no forces of attraction between them. They move randomly at high speeds in all directions, constantly colliding with each other and with the walls of their container. Gases have no fixed shape and no fixed volume — they spread out to fill whatever space is available.

Key Fact

Solid: particles in a fixed regular arrangement, vibrating about fixed positions, very close together. Liquid: particles close together but irregularly arranged, able to slide past each other. Gas: particles widely spaced, moving randomly at high speeds.

What Is Density?

Density tells you how much mass is packed into a given volume. A dense material has a lot of mass in a small space; a less dense material has the same volume but less mass. The equation for density is:

$$\rho = \frac{m}{V}$$

where \(\rho\) (the Greek letter rho) is density in kilograms per cubic metre (kg/m\(^3\)), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), and \(V\) is volume in cubic metres (m\(^3\)). Density can also be expressed in grams per cubic centimetre (g/cm\(^3\)).

For example, if a block of aluminium has a mass of 2.7 kg and a volume of 0.001 m\(^3\): \(\rho = \frac{2.7}{0.001} = 2700\) kg/m\(^3\). This means every cubic metre of aluminium contains 2700 kg of material.

Key Fact

Density = mass ÷ volume, or \(\rho = \frac{m}{V}\). Units: kg/m\(^3\) or g/cm\(^3\). You must be able to recall and rearrange this equation.

Density and States of Matter

The differences in density between solids, liquids, and gases can be explained using the particle model. In solids, particles are packed closely together in a regular arrangement, so there is a lot of mass in a small volume — giving solids a high density. In liquids, particles are still close together (though slightly further apart than in solids), so liquids have a similar density to solids, often just slightly lower.

In gases, particles are far apart with large gaps between them. The same number of particles occupies a much larger volume, so gases have a much lower density than solids or liquids. For example, the density of liquid water is about 1000 kg/m\(^3\), but the density of water vapour (steam at 100 \(^{\circ}\)C) is only about 0.6 kg/m\(^3\) — roughly 1600 times less dense.

Water is unusual because its solid form (ice) is less dense than its liquid form. When water freezes, the particles arrange themselves into a crystalline structure with gaps, making ice about 9% less dense than liquid water. This is why ice floats. Most other substances are denser as solids than as liquids.

Core Practical: Measuring Density

You need to know how to investigate the density of both regular and irregular solids, and of liquids.

Regular solid (e.g. a metal block): Use a balance to measure its mass in grams. Use a ruler or vernier calipers to measure its dimensions (length, width, height) and calculate the volume using \(V = l \times w \times h\). Then use \(\rho = \frac{m}{V}\) to calculate density.

Irregular solid (e.g. a pebble): Measure the mass on a balance. Fill a measuring cylinder with a known volume of water, lower the solid gently into the water, and record the new volume. The volume of the solid equals the rise in water level (new volume minus original volume). This is called the displacement method. Then use \(\rho = \frac{m}{V}\).

Liquid: Place an empty measuring cylinder on a balance and zero it (or record its mass). Pour in a known volume of liquid and record the mass. Then use \(\rho = \frac{m}{V}\).

When using a measuring cylinder, always read the volume at the bottom of the meniscus with your eye level with the liquid surface to avoid parallax error. Ensure irregular solids are fully submerged and that no air bubbles are trapped. For regular solids, measure each dimension in at least two places and take an average to reduce the effect of irregularities.

A metal cube has sides of 2.0 cm and a mass of 63.2 g. Calculate its density in g/cm\(^3\).

Volume \(= 2.0 \times 2.0 \times 2.0 = 8.0\) cm\(^3\).

Density \(= \frac{63.2}{8.0} = 7.9\) g/cm\(^3\).

This is close to the density of iron (7.87 g/cm\(^3\)), so the cube is likely made of iron or steel.

Key Fact

To measure the density of an irregular solid: (1) measure its mass on a balance, (2) use the displacement method with a measuring cylinder to find its volume, (3) calculate \(\rho = \frac{m}{V}\).

Exam Tip

Watch your units carefully. If mass is in grams and volume in cm\(^3\), density will be in g/cm\(^3\). If mass is in kg and volume in m\(^3\), density will be in kg/m\(^3\). To convert g/cm\(^3\) to kg/m\(^3\), multiply by 1000.

Summary

The particle model explains the properties of solids, liquids, and gases in terms of particle arrangement and movement. Density is mass per unit volume (\(\rho = m/V\)). Solids and liquids have high densities because particles are close together; gases have low densities because particles are far apart. The core practical requires you to measure density using mass balances, rulers, and displacement methods.

lessons.title: Changes of State & Internal Energy
lessons.description: Changes of state, internal energy, specific heat capacity, specific latent heat, energy transfer, and gas pressure relationships.
lessons.content_html:
Changes of State

Matter can change from one state to another when it is heated or cooled. These changes of state are physical changes, not chemical changes. The material keeps its original properties and the change can be reversed. For example, water can freeze into ice and then melt back into water — the substance is still water throughout.

The key changes of state are:

Melting — solid to liquid. Freezing — liquid to solid. Evaporation — liquid to gas (from the surface, at any temperature). Boiling — liquid to gas (throughout the liquid, at a specific temperature). Condensation — gas to liquid. Sublimation — solid directly to gas (without passing through the liquid state).

During any change of state, mass is conserved. No atoms are created or destroyed — the same particles are simply rearranged into a different structure. If you freeze 200 g of water, you get exactly 200 g of ice.

Key Fact

Changes of state are physical changes — they are reversible and mass is conserved. The six changes are: melting, freezing, evaporation, boiling, condensation, and sublimation.

Internal Energy and Heating

Every system stores energy in its particles. This internal energy is the total kinetic energy (from particle movement) and potential energy (from the forces between particles) of all the particles in the system.

When you heat a substance, you increase its internal energy. This can have two effects:

Temperature rises: If the substance is not changing state, the added energy increases the kinetic energy of the particles — they move faster (in liquids and gases) or vibrate more vigorously (in solids). The temperature goes up.

Change of state: If the substance is at its melting or boiling point, the added energy goes into breaking or weakening the bonds between particles (increasing potential energy), not into making them move faster. The temperature stays constant during the change of state, even though energy is still being transferred in.

Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles. During a change of state, all the energy being supplied goes into overcoming the forces of attraction between particles (increasing potential energy), not into increasing their speed. Since kinetic energy does not increase, the temperature remains constant until the change of state is complete.

Specific Heat Capacity

Specific heat capacity tells you how much energy is needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 \(^{\circ}\)C. Different materials have different specific heat capacities. Water has a high specific heat capacity (4200 J/kg \(^{\circ}\)C), meaning it takes a lot of energy to heat up — but it also releases a lot of energy when it cools down, which is why water is used in central heating systems.

The equation is:

$$\Delta Q = m \times c \times \Delta \theta$$

where \(\Delta Q\) is the change in thermal energy in joules (J), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), \(c\) is specific heat capacity in J/kg \(^{\circ}\)C, and \(\Delta \theta\) is the change in temperature in \(^{\circ}\)C.

For example, to heat 2 kg of water from 20 \(^{\circ}\)C to 100 \(^{\circ}\)C: \(\Delta Q = 2 \times 4200 \times (100 - 20) = 2 \times 4200 \times 80 = 672{,}000\) J (or 672 kJ).

Key Fact

\(\Delta Q = m \times c \times \Delta \theta\). Specific heat capacity (\(c\)) is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 \(^{\circ}\)C. Water: \(c\) = 4200 J/kg \(^{\circ}\)C.

Specific Latent Heat

Specific latent heat is the energy required to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without changing its temperature. There are two types:

Specific latent heat of fusion — the energy needed to change 1 kg of a substance from solid to liquid (or liquid to solid) at its melting point.

Specific latent heat of vaporisation — the energy needed to change 1 kg of a substance from liquid to gas (or gas to liquid) at its boiling point. The latent heat of vaporisation is always larger than the latent heat of fusion for the same substance, because the particles must completely overcome all forces of attraction to become a gas.

The equation is:

$$Q = m \times L$$

where \(Q\) is thermal energy for the change of state in joules (J), \(m\) is mass in kilograms (kg), and \(L\) is specific latent heat in joules per kilogram (J/kg).

To determine the specific heat capacity of water: place a known mass of water in an insulated container with an immersion heater. Record the starting temperature, switch on the heater for a measured time, and record the final temperature. Use the power rating of the heater and the time to calculate the energy supplied (\(E = P \times t\)), then rearrange \(\Delta Q = m \times c \times \Delta \theta\) to find \(c\).

For the temperature–time graph of melting ice: place crushed ice in a beaker and heat it steadily, recording the temperature every 30 seconds. The graph shows temperature rising, then a flat section at 0 \(^{\circ}\)C (while ice melts), then rising again. The flat section demonstrates that energy is being used to break bonds (latent heat) rather than raising temperature.

Reducing Unwanted Energy Transfer

Thermal insulation reduces unwanted energy transfer from warm objects to their surroundings. Houses lose thermal energy through walls, roofs, windows, and floors. Insulation methods include cavity wall insulation (trapping air in foam to reduce convection and conduction), loft insulation (fibreglass traps pockets of air), double glazing (two panes with a gap reduce conduction and convection), and draught excluders (reduce convection through gaps).

The principle behind all these methods is the same: they trap air. Air is a poor conductor, and when trapped in small pockets it cannot circulate (convect), making it an excellent insulator.

Gas Pressure and Temperature

The pressure of a gas is caused by particles colliding with the walls of their container. Each collision exerts a tiny force on the wall. The total of all these forces, divided by the area of the wall, gives the pressure.

When the temperature of a gas increases (at constant volume), the particles gain kinetic energy and move faster. They hit the walls more frequently and with greater force, so the pressure increases. Conversely, cooling a gas reduces particle speed and lowers the pressure.

Key Fact

Gas pressure is caused by particles colliding with container walls. Heating a gas at constant volume makes particles move faster, collide more frequently and with more force, so pressure increases.

Absolute Zero and the Kelvin Scale

Absolute zero is the lowest possible temperature: −273 \(^{\circ}\)C (or 0 K on the Kelvin scale). At absolute zero, particles have no kinetic energy and stop moving entirely. It is impossible to cool anything below this temperature.

To convert between Celsius and Kelvin:

$$\text{Temperature in K} = \text{Temperature in } ^{\circ}\text{C} + 273$$

For example, 100 \(^{\circ}\)C = 373 K, and 0 K = −273 \(^{\circ}\)C.

The Kelvin scale is an absolute scale that starts at absolute zero, where particle motion stops. This makes it directly proportional to the kinetic energy of particles. If you double the temperature in kelvin, you double the average kinetic energy. This relationship does not work with Celsius because 0 \(^{\circ}\)C is not the point of zero kinetic energy.

Exam Tip

When explaining why temperature stays constant during a change of state, always link it to potential energy increasing (bonds breaking or forming) while kinetic energy stays the same. Simply saying “energy is used to change state” is too vague.

Summary

Changes of state are reversible physical changes where mass is conserved. Heating can raise temperature (increasing kinetic energy) or cause a change of state (increasing potential energy at constant temperature). Specific heat capacity (\(\Delta Q = mc\Delta\theta\)) measures energy to change temperature. Specific latent heat (\(Q = mL\)) measures energy to change state. Gas pressure depends on particle collisions, and absolute zero (−273 \(^{\circ}\)C) is the point where particle motion stops.

The energy needed to change the state of 1 kg of a substance without changing its temperature, measured in J/kg.
The energy needed to change 1 kg between solid and liquid states at the melting point.
The energy needed to change 1 kg between liquid and gas states at the boiling point.
During a change of state, the total mass stays the same because no atoms are created or destroyed.
